title: Critical periods and developmental plasticity
text:
CHAPTER 11. PLASTICITY AND DEVELOPMENT
SECTION 11.1. CRITICAL PERIODS AND DEVELOPMENTAL PLASTICITY

How does a brain wire itself?

The human brain contains about 86 billion neurons and on the order of a hundred trillion synapses. The human genome contains roughly 20,000 protein-coding genes. There is no way the genome could specify every connection individually. Instead, the brain builds itself through a combination of genetically guided developmental programs and activity-dependent refinement, in which the patterns of neural activity, driven first by spontaneous activity and then by experience, sculpt the connections. This section explains these processes and the idea of critical periods: windows in development when experience has an especially strong and lasting effect. For an engineer, it is a story of a self-assembling, self-calibrating system; for an AI researcher, it raises questions about initialization, pretraining, and learning schedules.

Molecular guidance: the chemoaffinity hypothesis

In the 1940s, Roger Sperry performed experiments on frogs and newts, in which he cut the optic nerve and rotated the eye by 180 degrees. The optic nerve regenerated (as it can in amphibians), and the animals then behaved as if their visual world were upside down: when a fly was presented above, the animal struck downward, and this behavior never corrected with experience. Sperry concluded that the regenerating axons had grown back to their original targets in the optic tectum, regardless of the fact that this produced maladaptive behavior. In 1963 he formulated the chemoaffinity hypothesis: neurons carry molecular "identification tags" that guide their axons to specific targets.

This hypothesis was confirmed decades later with the discovery of guidance molecules. In the retinotectal system, gradients of ephrin ligands and their Eph receptors across the tectum and retina help map retinal positions onto tectal positions (work by Friedrich Bonhoeffer, John Flanagan, and others in the 1990s). Other families of axon guidance molecules, such as netrins, slits, and semaphorins, attract or repel growing axons. Growth cones, the motile tips of growing axons first described by Cajal, sense these cues and steer accordingly. Sperry shared the 1981 Nobel Prize with Hubel and Wiesel, though his share was for split-brain research.

Survival and pruning

Development also involves overproduction followed by elimination. Many more neurons are produced than survive; in some regions, roughly half of the neurons generated die during development by programmed cell death (apoptosis). Neurons compete for limited supplies of "trophic factors" released by their targets. Rita Levi-Montalcini and Stanley Cohen discovered the first such factor, nerve growth factor (NGF), in the 1950s, and shared the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Neurons that make good connections receive enough trophic support and survive; others die. This is a kind of selection process, which Gerald Edelman developed into a broader theory called "neural Darwinism."

Synapses are also overproduced and then pruned. Peter Huttenlocher's counts of synapses in human cortex, published from the late 1970s onward, suggested that synaptic density rises to a peak in early childhood and then declines over years, with the timing varying across cortical regions (earlier in visual cortex, later in prefrontal cortex). Pruning in prefrontal cortex continues into adolescence. Microglia participate in pruning by engulfing synapses, a process involving immune-system molecules (complement proteins), as shown by Beth Stevens and colleagues in the 2000s and 2010s.

Spontaneous activity before experience

Even before the eyes open, the developing visual system is active. In the 1990s, Carla Shatz, Marla Feller, Rachel Wong, Markus Meister, Denis Baylor, and colleagues showed that the developing retina generates spontaneous "retinal waves": bursts of activity that spread across the retina, so that neighboring ganglion cells fire together, while distant cells fire at different times. These correlated patterns carry information about which cells are neighbors and which eye they belong to. Blocking retinal waves disrupts the refinement of retinal projections into eye-specific layers in the LGN and the refinement of topographic maps. In other words, the developing visual system trains itself on internally generated "data" before it sees the world.

The principle that guides this refinement is Hebbian (section 7.1): inputs that are active together strengthen their connections onto common targets and outcompete inputs that are not correlated with them. Carla Shatz's slogan "cells that fire together wire together" was coined precisely in this context. Since the two eyes' waves are not synchronized with each other, Hebbian competition separates their inputs into eye-specific domains.

Critical periods in vision

Section 8.2 described the monocular deprivation experiments of Hubel and Wiesel. Closing one eye of a kitten during a critical period in early life caused the cortex to become dominated by the open eye, with lasting loss of vision through the deprived eye even after it was reopened. The same deprivation in adult cats had little effect. Several features of these experiments became central to the concept of a critical period:

- The effect depends on timing: there is a window of high sensitivity, which opens, peaks, and closes. In cats, sensitivity peaks around four to six weeks after birth and declines over the following months.
- Competition matters: closing both eyes produced less dramatic loss of cortical responses than closing one, because the two eyes' inputs were not competing unequally. This indicates that the deprived eye loses ground because the active eye wins a Hebbian competition, not merely because the deprived eye is inactive.
- Effects can be partly reversed during the critical period (for example, by reverse suture, opening the deprived eye and closing the other), but not after.

These findings have direct clinical relevance. Amblyopia, reduced vision in one eye due to abnormal visual experience in childhood (often caused by strabismus, unequal refractive errors, or cataracts), affects a few percent of people. Treatment, such as patching the stronger eye to force use of the weaker eye, is most effective in early childhood, consistent with a critical period, though some improvement is possible later. Children born with dense cataracts need early surgery to avoid permanent visual deficits.

Other critical periods

Critical periods have been described in many systems:

- Imprinting. Konrad Lorenz described in the 1930s how newly hatched geese follow the first moving object they see, normally their mother, and form a lasting attachment, but only during a short sensitive window after hatching. Lorenz shared the 1973 Nobel Prize with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Karl von Frisch.
- Birdsong. Young male zebra finches and other songbirds learn their songs by listening to an adult tutor during a sensitive period and then practicing, comparing their own output to a memorized template. Peter Marler, Fernando Nottebohm, Masakazu Konishi, and others studied song learning, which is a widely used model of vocal learning and has been compared to human speech acquisition.
- Sound localization in barn owls. Eric Knudsen showed that young barn owls fitted with prism goggles that shifted their visual field adjusted their auditory maps in the brain to match the shifted visual world, a process guided by vision. Young owls adapted much more readily than adults, though adults could adapt partially, especially with incremental training.
- Language. Children acquire native-like pronunciation and grammar of languages they are exposed to early much more easily than adults. Patricia Kuhl and colleagues showed that infants initially discriminate speech sounds from many languages but by around their first birthday become tuned to the sounds of their native language and less sensitive to non-native contrasts. Whether there is a strict critical period for language, and when it closes, is debated; the evidence suggests a gradual decline in some abilities (such as accent) rather than a sharp cutoff.
- Social and emotional development. Studies of children raised in severely deprived institutions, such as the Bucharest Early Intervention Project led by Charles Nelson, Nathan Fox, and Charles Zeanah, found that children placed in foster care earlier showed better outcomes in several domains than those placed later, consistent with sensitive periods for some aspects of development.

Mechanisms: what opens and closes critical periods?

Research since the 1990s, much of it by Takao Hensch, Lamberto Maffei, Michael Stryker, Mark Bear, and others, has identified mechanisms controlling critical periods in the visual cortex:

- Maturation of inhibition. Hensch and colleagues showed in the late 1990s that mice lacking an enzyme for synthesizing GABA (GAD65) did not show a normal critical period for ocular dominance plasticity, and that treatment with benzodiazepines (which enhance GABA-A receptor function) could trigger the critical period early. Specifically, the maturation of parvalbumin-expressing fast-spiking inhibitory interneurons appears to open the critical period. A certain level of inhibition seems necessary to make cortical circuits sensitive to competitive differences in input.
- Brakes on plasticity. As the critical period closes, molecular and structural "brakes" accumulate. Perineuronal nets, lattice-like structures of extracellular matrix that wrap around parvalbumin interneurons, form at the end of the critical period. Tommaso Pizzorusso, Lamberto Maffei, and colleagues showed in 2002 that degrading perineuronal nets with the enzyme chondroitinase ABC in adult rats reactivated ocular dominance plasticity. Myelin-associated proteins and their receptor (Nogo receptor) also limit plasticity; mice lacking the Nogo receptor retain ocular dominance plasticity into adulthood (Aaron McGee, Stephen Strittmatter, and colleagues, 2005). Lynx1, a protein that dampens nicotinic acetylcholine receptor signaling, is another brake.
- Neuromodulation. Acetylcholine, noradrenaline, and serotonin influence plasticity. For example, chronic treatment with the antidepressant fluoxetine was reported by Jose Fernando Maya Vetencourt, Maffei, and colleagues in 2008 to restore ocular dominance plasticity in adult rats.

These findings suggest that critical periods are not simply the result of a young brain being "more plastic" in general, but are actively regulated by circuit maturation and molecular brakes, which in principle could be manipulated. This has inspired research on treatments for amblyopia in adults and for recovery after brain injury, though translating these findings to humans is challenging.

Why have critical periods at all?

From an engineering perspective, why would a system limit its own ability to learn? Several reasons have been proposed:

- Stability. Once a basic representation has been learned, such as the mapping of the two eyes onto the cortex, later processing stages depend on it. If early stages kept changing, later stages would need to relearn constantly. Freezing early stages provides a stable foundation, a principle familiar from hierarchical systems.
- Efficiency. Plasticity has metabolic and structural costs, and maintaining it may be expensive.
- Protection. A brain that remains highly plastic could be overwritten by unusual or harmful experiences.
- Timing matched to the environment. Some features of the environment (such as the statistics of visual scenes or the sounds of the native language) are learned once and are stable for life, so it makes sense to learn them early and then lock them in.

Bridge to AI: initialization, pretraining, and critical periods in networks

Several parallels with AI are worth noting.

Spontaneous activity as pretraining. The developing brain trains itself on internally generated patterns, like retinal waves, before it receives real sensory data. This resembles pretraining a network on synthetic data or with self-supervised objectives before fine-tuning on real data. Some researchers have explored pretraining vision networks on procedurally generated images (for example, fractal patterns or random noise structures) and found that this can provide useful initial representations; this has been explicitly compared to retinal waves.

Critical learning periods in deep networks. As noted in section 8.2, Achille, Rovere, and Soatto (2019) found that deep networks exhibit critical periods: if a network is trained on blurred images early in training, it may never fully recover even after many epochs of training on clear images, while the same deficit introduced later has little lasting effect. They linked this to changes in the information stored in the weights, measured by the Fisher information, which rises early in training and then decreases. This suggests that critical periods may be a general property of learning systems that build hierarchical representations, not just a biological quirk.

Learning rate schedules and freezing. Many training procedures in deep learning use a high learning rate early and lower it later (learning rate decay), effectively closing a "critical period" for large changes. In transfer learning, engineers often freeze the early layers of a pretrained network (which encode general features like edges) and fine-tune only the later layers on a new task. This is strikingly similar to the brain's apparent strategy of stabilizing early sensory processing after development while keeping higher areas more plastic.

Overproduction and pruning. Neural network pruning methods remove unnecessary weights or units after training to make networks smaller and faster. Jonathan Frankle and Michael Carbin's 2019 "lottery ticket hypothesis" proposed that large, randomly initialized networks contain small subnetworks ("winning tickets") that, when trained in isolation from their original initialization, can match the performance of the full network. The analogy to developmental overproduction and pruning of synapses has been noted by many researchers, though the mechanisms are different.

Summary

- The genome cannot specify every synapse; brains develop through molecular guidance plus activity-dependent refinement.
- Sperry's chemoaffinity hypothesis (1963) was confirmed by guidance molecules such as ephrins and Eph receptors.
- Neurons and synapses are overproduced and then pruned, guided by trophic factors (NGF) and activity; microglia help prune synapses.
- Spontaneous retinal waves refine visual connections before eye opening, through Hebbian competition.
- Critical periods are windows of heightened sensitivity to experience, seen in ocular dominance, imprinting, birdsong, owl sound localization, language, and social development.
- Maturation of parvalbumin inhibitory interneurons opens the visual critical period, while perineuronal nets, Nogo receptor signaling, and other brakes close it; manipulating them can reopen plasticity in animals.
- Deep networks show critical learning periods; pretraining, learning rate schedules, layer freezing, and pruning have developmental analogs.
